concept.name: Chaos Engineering

relationships.description: Connects Chaos Engineering to system design hld architectures in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: Chaos engineering is the disciplined practice of injecting controlled, hypothesis-driven faults—like AZ blackholes, 200 ms packet delay, or Redis evictions—into production-like systems to uncover hidden fragility before real outages do.
spark.keyTakeaway: Chaos engineering is not random server killing: define a measurable steady-state hypothesis first, enforce strict blast-radius abort conditions, and run automated experiments in CI/GameDays to verify timeouts, retries, and fallbacks actually work.

concept.whyItMatters: Distributed systems rarely fail from a single clean crash; they fail from gray failures—a slow network switch adding 400 ms jitter, a half-open TLS socket, or a primary DB failover that triggers an exponential retry storm across 40 microservices. Unit tests and staging mocks never reproduce production connection-pool exhaustion or misconfigured circuit breakers. Chaos engineering surfaces these unknown unknowns proactively while engineers are awake and watching.
whenToUse: After implementing resilience patterns (circuit breakers, bulkheads, multi-AZ failover, read-replica promotion) to prove they actually trigger under real fault conditions.
During regular GameDays ahead of major traffic peaks (e.g., Black Friday, product launches) to validate runbooks, paging alerts, and graceful degradation.
In continuous delivery pipelines (staging/canary environments) to catch regressions such as removed timeouts or missing retry jitter.
whenNotToUse: When the system already lacks basic observability (metrics, distributed tracing, structured logs)—injecting faults without telemetry just creates an un-diagnosable outage.
When known, unfixed single points of failure exist (e.g., single-instance database with no backup or failover); fix the obvious architecture flaw before running experiments.
In production without automated abort triggers, RBAC guardrails, and leadership sign-off on an acceptable blast radius.
keyPoints: Every experiment starts with a **steady-state hypothesis** expressed in business or SLO metrics (e.g., 'Checkout success rate stays >=99.9% and P99 <=250 ms when 1 of 3 Kafka brokers is terminated').
Start with the smallest possible **blast radius** (a single canary pod or 1% synthetic traffic in staging), then graduate to production AZ-level faults only after lower-tier tests pass.
Automated **abort conditions** (stop-buttons) must immediately halt fault injection if error rates, P99 latency, or synthetic checkout probes breach safety thresholds.
Network and gray-failure injections (packet loss, 500 ms latency, DNS blackholing, CPU throttling) uncover far more real-world bugs than simple `kill -9` pod terminations.
The goal is organizational learning and automated verification—every uncovered weakness should result in a permanent fix (timeout, bulkhead, fallback) and a regression chaos test.

examples.title: Uncovering a Retry Storm via Downstream Latency Injection
examples.scenario: A fintech checkout service sets a 500 ms HTTP timeout on its Fraud-Scoring dependency with 3 automatic retries, assuming transient blips are handled safely.
examples.outcome: Injecting 600 ms of artificial latency to 10% of Fraud-Scoring pods via Chaos Mesh caused all 3 retries to trigger simultaneously, multiplying traffic to the Fraud DB by 4x and exhausting the checkout service's thread pool. The team added a 150 ms hedged-request/circuit-breaker limit, retry budgets (max 10% retry overhead), and jittered backoff.

examples.title: Multi-AZ Failover Verification in Kubernetes
examples.scenario: A payment gateway claimed full multi-AZ resilience across `ap-south-1a/b/c`, but had never tested an actual Availability Zone network partition.
examples.outcome: During a controlled GameDay using AWS Fault Injection Service (FIS) to blackhole traffic in `ap-south-1a`, engineers discovered that CoreDNS pods were pinned to `1a` via an old node selector and Envoy kept routing to stale endpoints for 45 seconds. Fixing pod topology spread constraints and active health-check eviction cut failover recovery from 45 seconds to 3.2 seconds.

tradeOffs.pro: Production chaos tests real traffic shapes, authentic data skew, and live third-party dependencies that staging can never replicate.
tradeOffs.con: Carries real user-impact risk if abort triggers fail or blast radius is misconfigured; requires mature observability and canary isolation.

tradeOffs.factor: Continuous Automated Chaos vs. Periodic GameDays
tradeOffs.pro: Automated chaos in CI/CD (e.g., LitmusChaos/Chaos Mesh) catches resilience regressions like missing timeouts on every release.
tradeOffs.con: GameDays build human muscle memory, test on-call runbooks, and uncover cross-team communication bottlenecks that automated scripts miss.

tradeOffs.pro: Infra faults (CPU stress, `tc` packet loss, AZ blackhole) validate kernel, DNS, and orchestration behavior cleanly.
tradeOffs.con: Application-level faults (fault-injection headers in Istio/Envoy, JVM exception injection) allow per-request scoping (`x-chaos-user: test`) with near-zero blast radius.

failureModes.name: Runaway Blast Radius
failureModes.description: A broad label selector (e.g., `app=payments` instead of `app=payments,track=canary`) injects 100% packet loss across all production replicas instead of 5%.
failureModes.mitigation: Enforce strict namespace/label RBAC in Chaos Mesh/Gremlin, require explicit `percentage` caps, and dry-run target selectors before execution.

failureModes.name: Missing Abort / Rollback Hook
failureModes.description: The chaos controller loses connectivity or crashes mid-experiment, leaving `iptables` drop rules or `tc netem` latency active on production nodes indefinitely.
failureModes.mitigation: Use time-bounded TTLs on all fault daemons (auto-revert after 120 seconds if controller heartbeat is lost) and wire Prometheus Alertmanager webhooks to abort immediately.

failureModes.name: Observability Blindness Under Load
failureModes.description: Fault injection saturates the network interface, which also drops Prometheus scrapes or OpenTelemetry spans—leaving engineers blind during the experiment.
failureModes.mitigation: Isolate telemetry/control-plane traffic on separate interfaces or exclude monitoring ports from `tc`/`iptables` fault rules.

failureModes.name: Testing Only Clean Crash-Stop Failures
failureModes.description: Teams only run `kubectl delete pod`, missing gray failures like clock skew, full disks, zombie processes, or 30% packet loss where health checks still pass.
failureModes.mitigation: Expand the experiment catalog to include asymmetric network partitions, DNS timeouts, disk I/O throttling, and dependency 503s.

commonMistakes: Running 'Chaos Monkey' randomly without a written steady-state hypothesis, turning engineering experiments into pointless firefighting.
Injecting faults during an existing incident, weekend skeleton crew, or peak business hours before lower-environment experiments have passed.
Forgetting to clean up side effects after an experiment (e.g., orphaned `tc` rules, stale DNS caches, or polluted test orders in production analytics).
Treating a failed chaos experiment as a failure of the chaos tool rather than a valuable discovery of a real production vulnerability.
Skipping the post-experiment remediation loop—discovering a missing timeout during a GameDay and never filing or prioritizing the fix.

sections.content:
## The idea

Chaos engineering is empirical verification for distributed systems. Rather than *assuming* that timeouts, retries, circuit breakers, and multi-AZ failovers will save you during an outage, you **prove** they work by injecting controlled turbulence into a running system.

Grounded in the scientific method, every chaos experiment follows four steps: (1) define the **steady state** using measurable SLOs, (2) hypothesize that the steady state holds under a specific fault, (3) inject the fault with a tightly bounded **blast radius** and automated **abort triggers**, and (4) observe the delta between expected and actual behavior to harden the architecture.

## Concrete walkthrough

Walk through a controlled latency-injection experiment on an e-commerce **Checkout Service** that calls an **Inventory Service**:

1. **Steady-State Baseline:** Confirm Checkout P99 latency is 180 ms and success rate is 99.95% over the last 15 minutes via Prometheus.
2. **Hypothesis:** If 10% of Inventory Service pods experience 800 ms network latency, Checkout's circuit breaker (configured for 300 ms timeout and 50% error threshold) should trip for those slow pods and fall back to cached stock status—keeping Checkout P99 <= 350 ms and success rate >= 99.5%.
3. **Scoped Injection:** Using **Chaos Mesh** (`NetworkChaos`) or **Istio `VirtualService`** fault injection, apply 800 ms delay (`tc netem`) strictly to pods matching `app=inventory,track=canary` for a max duration of 3 minutes, with an automated Prometheus abort webhook if Checkout 5xx exceeds 1%.
4. **Observation:** Metrics reveal Checkout P99 spikes to 1,200 ms and threads climb from 40 to 200—because the HTTP client had `readTimeout = 5000ms` overriding the circuit breaker's expectation!
5. **Remediation & Regression Gate:** Lower the HTTP client `readTimeout` to 250 ms, add a 10% retry budget, and add this exact experiment to the staging CI/CD pipeline.

sections.eyebrow: 03 / Fault taxonomy: crash-stop vs. gray failures
sections.content:
## Fault taxonomy: crash-stop vs. gray failures

Most teams start by killing pods (`PodChaos`), which only tests clean crash-stop behavior where Kubernetes immediately removes the pod IP from Service endpoints. Real outages are usually **gray failures**:

- **Network Asymmetric Delay & Packet Loss:** 300–1,000 ms `tc netem` delay or 5% packet drop keeps TCP connections alive just long enough to exhaust upstream worker pools.
- **DNS & Control-Plane Blackholes:** Blocking UDP/53 to CoreDNS or throttling Kubernetes API Server responses exposes services that re-resolve DNS on every request without caching.
- **Resource Starvation:** Cgroup CPU throttling (`stress-ng`) or disk I/O saturation (`blkio`) reveals noisy-neighbor sensitivity and lock-holder preemption.
- **State & Dependency Faults:** Redis `maxmemory` evictions, Kafka broker leader elections, and clock-skew (`adjtimex`) tests validate distributed consensus and token-expiry edge cases.

## Chaos tooling & blast-radius comparison

| Tool / Platform | Injection Layer | Key Strength | Safety / Abort Mechanism | Best Environment |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Chaos Mesh** | Kubernetes CRDs (`tc`, `iptables`, `stress-ng`) | Rich network/IO/JVM/time faults with clean UI | Time-bounded CRDs + webhook status checks | Kubernetes staging & production |
| **LitmusChaos** | Kubernetes + ChaosHub workflows | Deep Prometheus probe integration & CI/CD gates | Built-in `cmdProbe` / `promProbe` steady-state gates | GitOps & ArgoCD pipelines |
| **AWS Fault Injection Service (FIS)** | Cloud control plane (EC2, RDS, AZ, EKS) | Native AZ blackholes, RDS failovers, Spot interruptions | CloudWatch Alarm stop-conditions | Multi-AZ cloud resilience GameDays |
| **Istio / Envoy Fault Injection** | L7 Service Mesh (`x-chaos-*` headers) | Zero-blast-radius per-user or per-header HTTP faults | Scoped strictly to synthetic test headers | Production canary & shadow traffic |

## Failure modes

- **Unbounded Selector Blast Radius:** Applying a fault to all pods in a namespace instead of a 5% canary slice.
- **Orphaned Kernel Faults:** A crashed chaos agent leaves `tc netem` or `iptables` rules active after the experiment ends.
- **Telemetry Starvation:** Injecting 100% network loss on a node cuts off Prometheus/Datadog metrics, masking the actual failure.
- **Cascading Retry Amplification:** Testing a 200 ms delay reveals that 4 microservice hops each retrying 3 times turn 1 user request into `3^4 = 81` backend calls.

## GameDays & continuous verification

To turn chaos engineering into measurable reliability:

1. **Graduate by Environment:** Run destructive experiments in ephemeral/staging environments first, then move to L7 header-scoped production tests, and finally scheduled production GameDays.
2. **Score Every GameDay:** Track **Time to Detect (TTD)**, **Time to Mitigate (TTM)**, whether the right on-call team was paged, and whether dashboards showed the root cause within 3 minutes.
3. **Automate Regression Gates:** Every time a GameDay uncovers a bug (e.g., missing timeout or broken PDB), encode that exact fault as an automated Litmus/Chaos Mesh step in your pre-prod release pipeline.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Verify full observability (golden signals: latency, traffic, errors, saturation) before running any chaos experiment.
- [ ] Write an explicit steady-state hypothesis with quantitative SLO bounds before injecting faults.
- [ ] Configure automated abort triggers (Prometheus/CloudWatch alarms) and hard TTLs on every fault resource.
- [ ] Test gray failures (latency, packet loss, DNS blackhole, RDS failover)—not just `kubectl delete pod`.
- [ ] Document every uncovered weakness in a blameless post-experiment review and convert fixed issues into automated CI chaos regression tests.

interviewProblems.title: Chaos Engineering
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on Chaos Engineering. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Chaos engineering is the disciplined practice of injecting controlled, hypothesis-driven faults—like AZ blackholes, 200 ms packet delay, or Redis evictions—into production-like systems to uncover hidden fragility before real outages do.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: SLO & Telemetry Gate applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Automated Abort & Fix.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Automated Abort & Fix experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Enforce strict namespace/label RBAC in Chaos Mesh/Gremlin, require explicit `percentage` caps, and dry-run target selectors before execution.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Chaos engineering is not random server killing: define a measurable steady-state hypothesis first, enforce strict blast-radius abort conditions, and run automated experiments in CI/GameDays to verify timeouts, retries, and fallbacks actually work.
Avoid trap: Running 'Chaos Monkey' randomly without a written steady-state hypothesis, turning engineering experiments into pointless firefighting.
Avoid trap: Injecting faults during an existing incident, weekend skeleton crew, or peak business hours before lower-environment experiments have passed.
When to reach for it: After implementing resilience patterns (circuit breakers, bulkheads, multi-AZ failover, read-replica promotion) to prove they actually trigger under real fault conditions.
When to reach for it: During regular GameDays ahead of major traffic peaks (e.g., Black Friday, product launches) to validate runbooks, paging alerts, and graceful degradation.

putItTogether.title: Putting Chaos Engineering Together
putItTogether.summary: Chaos engineering is not random server killing: define a measurable steady-state hypothesis first, enforce strict blast-radius abort conditions, and run automated experiments in CI/GameDays to verify timeouts, retries, and fallbacks actually work.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Chaos Engineering before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Injecting 600 ms of artificial latency to 10% of Fraud-Scoring pods via Chaos Mesh caused all 3 retries to trigger simultaneously, multiplying traffic to the Fraud DB by 4x and exhausting the checkout service's thread pool. The team added a 150 ms hedged-request/circuit-breaker limit, retry budgets (max 10% retry overhead), and jittered backoff.
